questions.question: Why can the B-mode power spectrum not distinguish matter bounce from inflation in the setup described?

options.A: Both produce the same-form B-mode power spectrum, although their superhorizon tensor perturbations evolve differently
options.B: Both produce identically zero B-mode power because only scalars source polarization
options.C: The transfer functions erase all tensor information in both paradigms
options.D: The power spectra differ only by an overall sign

questions.rationale: The authors motivate the bispectrum because bounce perturbations grow outside the horizon while inflationary perturbations freeze.
questions.evidence_quote: the power spectrum due to matter bounce has the same form

questions.question: What parity and multipole conditions does the paper state for a nonzero B-mode auto-bispectrum?

options.A: Σli must be odd and all three li must be different
options.B: Σli must be even and at least two li equal
options.C: All li must be odd and consecutive
options.D: Only squeezed configurations with l1=l2+l3 contribute

questions.rationale: The Wigner-symbol properties impose both restrictions before numerical evaluation.
questions.evidence_quote: only for ∑li = odd, the B-mode auto-bispectrum in Eq. (8) is nonzero

questions.question: How many multipole triples did the authors consider at Σli=33, and what symmetry reduced the work?

options.A: 114 triples; permutation symmetry reduced evaluation to one of six permutations
options.B: 33 triples; parity reduced evaluation by a factor of three
options.C: 114 triples; only even permutations were allowed
options.D: 216 triples; Wigner 3j symmetry reduced computation by 1/114

questions.rationale: The sum constraint leaves 114 possibilities, while permutation-related bispectra differ only by a phase.
questions.evidence_quote: This implies 114 possibilities in total for the triple (l1,l2,l3).

questions.question: Which angular-momentum inequalities restrict the allowed (li,Li,l′i) combinations in the numerical integral?

options.B: li+Li≤l′i and l1+l2+l3 must be even
options.C: Li=li−l′i only, with no triangle condition

questions.rationale: The Wigner 3j and 9j symbols impose triangle constraints that prune integrations.

questions.question: How does the paper distinguish separable from inseparable bispectrum integrals computationally?

options.A: The form is separable when the denominator lacks kt=Σki; otherwise a Laplace transform introduces y and an e⁻ᵏʸ factor
options.B: Separable integrals use five variables, while inseparable ones use only x
options.C: The distinction depends on whether the Wigner 9j symbol vanishes
options.D: Inseparable forms omit transfer functions and use direct Monte Carlo sampling

questions.rationale: The presence of the summed-momentum denominator determines whether an auxiliary Laplace variable is needed.
questions.evidence_quote:
If it is absent, we will call bispec-
trum as separable

questions.question: What practical limitation led the authors to switch Wigner-symbol software for larger multipoles?

options.A: fgsl produced segmentation faults at larger l, so wigxjpf was used for high-l bispectrum evaluation
options.B: wigxjpf could not compute 9j symbols, so all calculations used fgsl
options.C: Rasch symmetry failed for even l, requiring hand-calculated symbols
options.D: Both libraries were limited to l≤16

questions.rationale: They used fgsl initially but reported a large-l failure and used wigxjpf thereafter.
questions.evidence_quote: fgsl gives segmentation fault at larger values of l.

questions.question: At r=0.01, where do the largest bispectrum amplitudes occur, and how do their magnitudes compare?

options.A: At permutations of (2,15,16); inflation is about 6×10⁻¹¹ while bounce is about 5×10⁻²³
options.B: At (11,11,11); inflation is 5×10⁻²³ while bounce is 6×10⁻¹¹
options.C: At (2,15,16); the two are equal after normalization
options.D: At permutations of (1,16,16); bounce is 10 times larger

questions.rationale: The peak location matches, but the bounce amplitude is around twelve orders smaller.
questions.evidence_quote: the peaks of the bispectrum in both cases appear at the permutations of (l1,l2,l3) = (2,15,16).

questions.question: What signal-to-noise values does the paper report for r=0.01 and lmax=100?

options.A: About 10⁻⁵ for inflation and 10⁻¹⁸ for bounce
options.B: About 10⁻¹⁸ for inflation and 10⁻⁵ for bounce

questions.rationale: The matter-bounce SNR is roughly 10⁻¹³ times the inflation value at these settings.
questions.evidence_quote:
lmax = 100, the SNR due to standard inﬂation turns out to be
∼10−5, whereas for bounce it is ∼10−18.

questions.question: What numerical integration cross-check did the authors report for the auxiliary x (and y) integrals?

options.A: Trapezoidal and rectangular integration gave the same answer
options.B: Only Gaussian quadrature converged, while trapezoidal diverged
options.C: Monte Carlo and Simpson methods agreed within 1%
options.D: The x integral was analytic, so no numerical cross-check was made

questions.rationale: The conclusion states that both rectangle and trapezoid integration produced matching values.
questions.evidence_quote: both the trapezoidal and rectangular integration methods were giving the same answer.

questions.question: What limitation does the paper emphasize about detectability of the matter-bounce B-mode bispectrum?

options.A: Its SNR is roughly 10⁻¹³ of inflation's for the quoted setup, making it even harder to detect
options.B: Its shape is identical to inflation, preventing theoretical comparison
options.C: It is detectable only for r=0.01 and lmax=100
options.D: The tensor transfer functions vanish for all allowed triangles

questions.rationale: Despite different shape functions, the signal amplitude and SNR are dramatically smaller than inflation's.
questions.evidence_quote: This means that it would be even more difficult to detect signals due to bounce as compared to inflation.
